title: Closing thoughts on love and thanks
summary: Jackson says musicians should learn to love, which frees the mind and shows in the playing; Hinton thanks him and ends the interview.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: Well, unless there's something else you want to tell me, I think we should wind this up.

I think you've done a marvelous job, and I can't thank you for sharing your life with me and the rest of the world that young people in the future might know what a real truly great musician is like and what kind of great obstacles you've overcome in these 40 or 50 years in which you've been in this business and still.

Well, you see, there's only one thing more I want to say, Milt, that there should -- everyone in this world, especially musicians, should learn more about love of their fellow man. And love will also help make you a good musician --
Right.
-- because you will portray this in your playing.
Music is love.
Oh, definitely it is.
Is love.
Definitely it is. And any young musician starting out now, please, learn to love because that will give you freedom of mind, freedom of thought, because
you have no time for any hatreds or any discrepancies of mind.
Yeah, it takes away from your talent, --
Exactly.
-- this time that you spend disliking someone you could be enjoying and playing and --
Exactly, exactly. You can enjoy the beauty of life.
Right.
And that's where it's at.

Well, thank you, and I hope that in time immemorial, in years to come, that your contribution to society, your contribution to music, you contribution to this great American art form, jazz, will be known and will be appreciated by all those who will listen to your oral history.
Thank you, Quentin Jackson.
Thank you, Milton, and thank you for ever being associated with me.
It's been my pleasure, Milt Hinton, all the way.
Good. Thank you so much.
(End of Proceedings as recorded.)
